first.rationale: Competitor pricing pressure makes promotional_pricing tempting, but memory_73 explicitly warns it reduced 30-day retention and should not be generalized as a growth strategy despite short-term acquisition gains—pursuing it risks sustainable qualified revenue, the stated objective. Activation and onboarding completion are both down this quarter, and two independent durable memories (memory_31, memory_86) support onboarding simplification as a reliable lever for activation and time-to-value with no noted downside. Since only one experiment slot is available, simplify_onboarding addresses two degrading metrics simultaneously with the strongest, least risky evidence base. I verify memory_73 to confirm the retention harm was material enough to rule out promotional pricing under competitive pressure, and memory_86 to confirm the onboarding evidence is robust before committing the week's only slot. Result should be scoped as a standard experiment rather than broad rollout, since inherited memory reflects prior contexts and current environment (competitor dynamics, declining trend) may shift effect sizes.

final.rationale: Verification confirms memory_73: the 40% targeted discount drove +31% signup and +18% qualified revenue but a -12% hit to 30-day retention, meaning the acquired cohort largely fails to survive the first renewal cycle. That is a direct threat to sustainable long-term qualified revenue, the stated objective, so promotional_pricing is ruled out despite the competitive pressure from the rival's entry pricing—chasing price-sensitive share this way would likely repeat the same value destruction. Verification of memory_86 confirms the onboarding-shortening result is robust and even positive for retention (completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, 30-day retention +3%), with no downside noted, and it's corroborated independently by memory_31's signup-simplification finding. This directly targets the two concrete degrading metrics this quarter (activation -6%, onboarding completion -4%) with a lever that has demonstrated durable, retention-positive effects rather than a short-term acquisition spike that erodes value. I'm scoping this as a standard experiment rather than broad rollout because current conditions (competitive pressure, declining baseline trends) differ from the original test context, so effect sizes should be reconfirmed before wider deployment. Enterprise_sales_assist and referral_incentive remain plausible future candidates but don't address this week's most acute, evidence-backed opportunity as directly.
